tldr: On tables, a well-tuned gradient-boosted tree ensemble is still the model to beat.
A probability is only useful if it's calibrated. Check a reliability diagram before you trust a score.
Conformal prediction wraps any model in intervals or sets with a guaranteed coverage rate.
takeaways: Expected test error = bias² + variance + noise. Capacity trades the first two; nothing beats the third.
Past the interpolation threshold, adding parameters can reduce test error (double descent). Implicit regularization decides which solution you get.
Boosting is gradient descent in function space: each tree fits the negative gradient of the loss.
Small learning rate + many trees + early stopping on validation data beats big steps. Your baseline for any table is a GBDT.
Accuracy ≠ calibration. Fit Platt, isotonic or temperature scaling on held-out data to make confidences honest.
Split conformal: take a quantile of held-out residuals and get ≥ 1−α coverage for any model. The guarantee is marginal, so check your subgroups.
SHAP explains the model, not the world. Correlated features split credit unpredictably.
Tabular foundation models (TabPFN) do in-context learning on small tables in one forward pass, and often beat tuned GBDTs there.
myths: Deep learning beats everything now.
On typical tabular benchmarks, tuned tree ensembles still often win, and they're cheaper to train and serve.
A predicted 0.9 means a 90% chance.
Only if the model is calibrated. Many models, including modern neural nets, are systematically over-confident.
High feature importance means the feature causes the outcome.
Importance (and SHAP) describes what the model relies on. Causal claims need causal assumptions or experiments.
cards: What does each new tree fit in gradient boosting?
The pseudo-residuals: the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions (y − p for log loss).
Why doesn't temperature scaling change accuracy?
Dividing every logit by the same T > 0 preserves their order, so the argmax (and the accuracy) are unchanged.
What does conformal prediction assume?
Only that calibration and test points are exchangeable (e.g. i.i.d.). Nothing about the model or the distribution.
What is the interpolation threshold?
The capacity at which a model can just fit the training data exactly. Test error spikes there under double descent.
Name two SHAP pitfalls.
Credit split arbitrarily between correlated features, and evaluating the model off the data manifold (interventional SHAP).
When would you pick TabPFN over a GBDT?
Small datasets (≲10k rows), little tuning time, and when calibrated probabilities matter. Pick the GBDT for huge tables and tight CPU latency.

tldr: Backprop is the chain rule applied in reverse topological order, about one extra pass for all gradients.
Deep nets train because of init + normalization + residual connections, plus a good optimizer and LR schedule.
Loss follows power laws in parameters, data and compute, which tells you how to spend a budget.
takeaways: Reverse-mode autodiff gives every gradient of a scalar loss for roughly the cost of a forward pass, at the price of storing activations.
Trainability comes from variance-preserving init, (pre-)normalization, and residual streams that carry gradients straight through.
AdamW (Adam + decoupled weight decay) is the default for transformers. L2 inside Adam is not the same thing.
Muon orthogonalizes the momentum of 2-D weight matrices. It's a strong 2025-era alternative for hidden layers.
The learning rate is hyperparameter #1. Use warmup, then cosine or WSD decay, and clip gradients.
Grokking: generalization can arrive long after memorization, and weight decay is what pushes the model there.
Compute-optimal training scales N and D together (~20 tokens/param), but production models over-train small models because inference is what costs money.
myths: Training loss hit zero, so we're done.
Grokking shows the most important learning can happen after memorization, driven by regularization.
Adam + L2 regularization = AdamW.
In Adam, the L2 gradient is divided by √v, so heavily-updated weights barely decay. AdamW decays the weights directly.
For a fixed budget, always train the biggest model you can.
Chinchilla showed many big models were under-trained. Splitting compute between parameters and tokens gives lower loss.
cards: Why do frameworks accumulate gradients with +=?
A value used in several places receives a gradient contribution from each use. The chain rule sums them.
What does LR warmup protect against?
Huge, noisy early updates while the weights and Adam's second-moment estimates are still far from equilibrium.
He initialization variance for ReLU layers?
Var(w) = 2 / fan_in, which keeps activation variance roughly constant through depth.
Muon's idealized update for momentum M = UΣVᵀ?
UVᵀ: the same matrix with every singular value set to 1, approximated cheaply with Newton–Schulz iterations.
What's the Chinchilla rule of thumb?
Roughly 20 training tokens per parameter at the compute-optimal point. Both N and D grow ~√C.
Why pre-norm instead of post-norm?
Pre-norm (x + F(Norm(x))) keeps the residual stream an untouched sum, which stabilizes very deep stacks.

tldr: Attention is a soft, differentiable dictionary lookup: softmax(QKᵀ/√d)·V.
Modern blocks = pre-norm RMSNorm + RoPE + SwiGLU + GQA, run with FlashAttention.
Generation is memory-bound: the KV cache, sampling, speculation and quantization decide speed and quality.
takeaways: Attention lets every token read from every earlier token, weighted by query–key match. The causal mask stops it from reading the future.
Scale logits by 1/√d<sub>k</sub> so the softmax doesn't saturate and gradients keep flowing.
RoPE rotates q and k by position, so scores depend only on relative offset.
The KV cache trades memory for compute. At long context it dominates serving cost, which is why GQA and latent attention exist.
Decoding settings (temperature, top-p, min-p) shape the output's character as much as fine-tuning does.
Speculative decoding is exact: the target model's distribution is preserved; only the speed depends on the draft model.
MoE separates parameters (memory) from FLOPs per token, and needs load balancing so experts don't collapse.
SSMs give linear-time, constant-memory sequence modeling. Input-dependent selectivity is what makes them work, and hybrids with attention are common.
myths: Greedy decoding gives the best output.
Greedy decoding tends to loop and produce bland text. Moderate-temperature sampling is usually better, and enables voting.
A 671B-parameter MoE only needs the memory of its 37B active parameters.
Every expert must be stored and served. MoE saves FLOPs per token, not memory.
Quantization loses a little precision everywhere, evenly.
A few outlier weights can wreck a per-tensor scale. Group-wise scales and outlier-aware methods are essential.
cards: Why divide attention logits by √d<sub>k</sub>?
Dot products of d-dim unit-variance vectors have variance d. Scaling keeps the softmax out of its saturated, zero-gradient regime.
KV-cache size per token?
2 (K and V) × layers × KV heads × head dim × bytes per element.
What does grouped-query attention share?
Each K/V head is shared by a group of query heads, shrinking the KV cache by (query heads / KV heads).
Speculative decoding acceptance rule?
Accept the draft token with probability min(1, p(x)/q(x)); on rejection, resample from the normalized max(0, p − q).
Why can Mamba train with a parallel scan?
Its recurrence is linear in the hidden state, so steps compose associatively and can be combined in a tree.
What is an induction head?
A head that finds the earlier occurrence of the current token and copies what came next, a core in-context-learning circuit.
equations: \langle R_m q, R_n k\rangle = \langle q, R_{n-m} k\rangle
h_t = \bar A_t h_{t-1} + \bar B_t x_t,\ y_t = C_t h_t

tldr: Generation = transporting noise to data along a learned vector field.
Flow matching regresses the velocity of straight noise→data paths, then samples by solving an ODE.
Guidance steers samples; latents + DiTs scale them up; CLIP connects images and text.
takeaways: Diffusion, score models and flow matching are one family: a time-dependent field that carries a simple distribution to the data distribution.
Flow-matching loss: regress v<sub>θ</sub>(x<sub>t</sub>, t) onto x₁ − x₀. Training needs no simulation and is about as simple as it gets.
Sampling is ODE solving. Fewer steps are faster but blurrier; reflow and distillation fix that.
Classifier-free guidance trades diversity for fidelity: (1+w)·conditional − w·unconditional.
Latent diffusion + diffusion transformers (DiT) are the scalable recipe for images and video.
CLIP's contrastive loss builds a shared image–text space, which gives you zero-shot classification and retrieval.
Vision-language models feed vision-encoder tokens into an LLM through a small projector.
myths: Diffusion models need hundreds of steps.
Distillation, consistency models and straighter flows bring high-quality sampling down to 1–4 steps.
Higher guidance is always better.
Large w over-saturates images and collapses diversity. It's a knob to tune, not a dial to max out.
VAEs are obsolete.
VAEs are the compressor inside most latent diffusion systems. They're still doing important work.
cards: What's the conditional flow-matching regression target?
The straight-path velocity x₁ − x₀ (data minus noise) at the point x<sub>t</sub> = (1−t)x₀ + t x₁.
Why does 1-step sampling land on the data mean?
At t = 0 the noisy point carries no information about its destination, so the optimal velocity points to E[x₁].
What does label dropout enable?
One network learns both conditional and unconditional predictions, which is what classifier-free guidance needs.
Where do CLIP's negatives come from?
The other N−1 pairs in the batch. Bigger batches give more and harder negatives.
What did DiT replace?
The UNet denoiser, with a plain transformer over patches of the latent. It scales predictably, like LLMs.
What does reflow do?
It re-pairs noise with the model's own outputs and retrains, which straightens trajectories so few-step sampling works.

tldr: Post-training (SFT → preferences → RL) turns a pretrained autocomplete into an assistant, and then a reasoner.
RL with verifiable rewards + GRPO produced reasoning models; test-time compute is the second scaling axis.
An agent is an LLM in a loop with tools. MCP standardizes the tools, and evals tell you if any of it works.
takeaways: Knowledge mostly comes from pretraining. Post-training shapes behaviour: format, helpfulness, judgment, reasoning.
LoRA learns a low-rank update ΔW = (α/r)·BA. Merge it for zero latency; QLoRA keeps the frozen base in 4-bit.
DPO optimizes preference pairs directly, with no reward model and no RL loop, anchored to a reference model.
GRPO: sample a group, normalize rewards within it, and push up the better-than-average answers. No critic needed.
Test-time compute (longer thinking, voting, verifiers) buys accuracy, especially where answers can be checked.
An agent is a while loop: think → call tool → observe. MCP lets any client use any tool server.
Treat everything an agent reads as data, not instructions. Prompt injection is the top agent risk.
Write evals before you optimize, and read your failures every week.
Sparse autoencoders pull interpretable features out of superposition, and adding a feature's direction can steer the model.
myths: Fine-tuning is the best way to teach a model new facts.
For facts, retrieval (RAG) is usually cheaper, fresher and citable. Fine-tune for behaviour, format and style.
A reasoning model's chain of thought shows exactly how it got its answer.
It's text shaped by RL. It's often useful, but it isn't guaranteed to be a faithful account of the computation.
You need a big framework to build an agent.
The core is a short loop around tool calls. Spend your effort on tools, evals and guardrails.
cards: Trainable parameters LoRA adds to a d_in × d_out matrix?
r · (d_in + d_out), compared with d_in · d_out for full fine-tuning.
GRPO advantage for sample i?
Â<sub>i</sub> = (r<sub>i</sub> − mean(r)) / std(r), computed within the group of answers to the same prompt.
Why does DPO keep a reference model?
The log-ratio to π<sub>ref</sub> acts as an implicit KL anchor (strength β), so the policy can't drift arbitrarily far.
What does MCP standardize?
How AI applications discover and call tools, read resources and use prompts exposed by external servers.
What is superposition?
Representing more features than dimensions by using nearly-orthogonal directions, which works because features are sparse.
When does majority voting hurt?
When one particular wrong answer is more likely than the right one. Voting then locks in the error.
